summary: Describes what network elements must do to deliver Guaranteed service, which gives applications firm limits on delay and a reserved amount of bandwidth. It is for applications that need predictable timing.

plainLanguage.summary: Guaranteed service defines how network elements can provide a firm upper limit on queueing delay for a flow. The flow must stay within its traffic description, and every element on the path must support the service.

questions: what is guaranteed service in intserv
how is end to end queueing delay bounded
what are the c and d error terms
what is a tspec and rspec
subtitle: A flow receives a provable upper bound on queueing delay and queue loss.

tldr.problem: Some applications need a firm bound on when datagrams arrive, while ordinary best-effort forwarding makes no delay promise.
tldr.mechanism: A flow describes its traffic with a token bucket and requests a service rate. Each network element reports error terms that contribute to the end-to-end delay bound.
tldr.outcome: Conforming traffic receives reserved bandwidth, bounded queueing delay, and no queue-overflow loss when each path element supports the service.

today: RFC 2212 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1997. It defines network-element behavior and points to RFC 2210 for RSVP usage.

sections.title: What Guaranteed Service Promises
sections.content:
RFC 2212 specifies the behavior network elements need to provide guaranteed service. A flow describes its traffic, and each network element returns information about how it handles that traffic.

Combining the information along the path gives an end-to-end bound on queueing delay. The RFC does not define how a reservation is set up or how a flow is identified; RSVP, manual configuration, or network management may provide that work.
sections.plainLanguage: The service lets an application request a bandwidth level and determine a maximum queueing delay. It defines router behavior, not the reservation setup method.

sections.title: End-to-End Behavior
sections.content:
A conforming flow receives an assured bandwidth level, bounded queueing delay, and no queueing loss, assuming network elements do not fail and routing does not change. The service controls maximum queueing delay, not minimum or average delay.

To know the full delivery delay, the application also needs path latency and adds it to the queueing bound. Since the guarantee covers rare long delays, many datagrams may arrive early and need buffering before playback.
sections.plainLanguage: The guarantee limits the longest time spent waiting in queues. It does not set the average delay or remove the fixed travel time across the path.

sections.title: Approximating a Dedicated Rate
sections.content:
Each network element must approximate a fluid model: a flow receives the service of a dedicated wire at rate R, independent of other flows. For a token bucket with rate r and depth b, ideal queueing delay is bounded by b/R when R is at least r.

Real elements report deviations as C, a rate-dependent term, and D, a rate-independent delay term. The local queueing bound is less than b/R + C/R + D. Conforming datagrams must not be fragmented by the service.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router estimates how far its service differs from an ideal dedicated link. The flow's delay bound includes those differences along with its traffic burst and reserved rate.

sections.title: Describing Traffic and Requested Service
sections.content:
The TSpec describes traffic with token-bucket rate r and depth b, peak rate p, minimum policed unit m, and maximum datagram size M. The RSpec requests service rate R and slack S; R MUST be at least r and S MUST be nonnegative.

The rate ranges from 1 byte per second to 40 terabytes per second, and bucket depth from 1 byte to 250 gigabytes. The slack term is measured in microseconds. An element derives its needed buffer; the RSpec does not carry a buffer-size field.
sections.plainLanguage: The traffic specification describes how fast data may arrive and how large bursts can be. The service request gives a reserved rate and any extra delay the application can accept.

sections.title: Adding Delay Terms Along the Path
sections.content:
Each network element reports C in bytes and D in microseconds. The C term is divided by the reserved rate R when calculating delay; D is already a time value. The path totals are Ctot and Dtot.

For an unspecified peak rate, the end-to-end queueing bound is b/R + Ctot/R + Dtot. The setup mechanism that collects and distributes these values is outside this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each hop reports two kinds of delay contribution. Adding them across the path lets an endpoint calculate a maximum queueing delay.

sections.title: Policing and Reshaping Traffic
sections.content:
Policing compares incoming traffic with its TSpec and is performed at the network edge. Reshaping delays traffic until it conforms again and is used at certain branch and merge points. Inside the network, an element that wants to police traffic MUST reshape it instead.

Nonconforming datagrams SHOULD receive best-effort service rather than simply being discarded. Dropping them could let a reservation with an inadequate traffic specification interrupt another receiver's best-effort traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The network checks traffic at its edge and can delay bursts inside the network until they fit the agreed pattern. Excess traffic should fall back to best-effort service.

items.title: C
items.text: Rate-dependent error, measured in bytes and divided by the reserved rate.

items.title: D
items.text: Rate-independent delay variation, measured in microseconds.

items.title: Ctot and Dtot
items.text: The corresponding sums over the path.
